task.title: Make harness roadmap mutations git-durable — fetch+rebase, commit, push the rmap status transition
acceptance_criteria: Every harness-driven `rmap status` transition on a project's canonical `roadmap/tasks.toml` (in_progress at dispatch start; done/pending at settle) is a durable git operation, not an uncommitted local-file write.

Before mutating, harness fetches and rebases the roadmap working copy onto the project's target branch so it never writes from a stale on-disk copy (the discipline rmap.md mandates for human writers).
After mutating, harness commits the tasks.toml change (subject e.g. `roadmap: task <id> -> <status>`) and pushes to the target branch.

Concurrent writers (sibling Claude sessions, cloud agents, other harness runs) no longer silently clobber each other's roadmap edits — verified by an integration test that interleaves two transitions against the same file.
A non-ff push (a second writer landed first) is handled by re-fetch+rebase+retry, not force-push; persistent conflict surfaces an error, never a blind overwrite.
Mechanical git substrate only — no judgment branch added to harness code.
out_of_scope: The single-Postgres settings consolidation (Task 208) — orthogonal.
Moving the roadmap out of TOML/git into Postgres — tasks.toml stays the canonical git-versioned source of truth.
task.body:
The multi-writer hazard rmap.md documents for human sessions also applies to harness itself, and just bit us: a sibling Claude session held a stale copy of `tasks.toml` and clobbered this session's phase-17 additions (recovered by hand).

harness's dispatch lifecycle mutates the CANONICAL `roadmap/tasks.toml` — `rmap status <id> in_progress` at dispatch start, `done`/`pending` at settle — but treats those mutations as ephemeral local-file writes: it does NOT fetch+rebase the working copy before writing, does NOT commit the transition, and does NOT push it. So every harness run is a silent, uncommitted concurrent writer racing every other session and cloud agent against the same shared file. rmap's validate-then-write guards against INVALID writes, not LOST ones — two valid writers still overwrite each other.

The roadmap status transition is pure mechanical git (fetch, rebase, commit one file, ff-push, retry-on-non-ff) — it fits the agent-gate principle that harness code is mechanical substrate only, no judgment. Make the transition durable and rebase-before-write so the canonical roadmap stops drifting uncommitted across writers.

Open design point for the implementer: where the roadmap mutation runs (main checkout vs the run's isolated worktree) and whether the push target is the project's `target_branch`. rmap walks ancestors to find `roadmap/tasks.toml`; pin the mutation+commit to a single well-defined checkout so the rebase semantics are unambiguous.
task.implemented: Harness.Roadmap.Durable makes every harness rmap status transition a durable git op: fetch target -> mutate fresh detached worktree at origin/<target> -> commit 'roadmap: task <id> -> <status>' -> ff-push (non-ff re-fetch+replay+retry, never --force) -> ff the operator's LOCAL target via shared Harness.Git.TargetSync so on-disk tasks.toml never drifts behind origin (the out-of-sync/merge-break the user flagged). All four Roadmap.mark_* mutators consolidated through one mutate/4 chokepoint; durable when a %Project{} with target_branch+local source is passed, else local rmap write. TargetSync extracted from Lander.sync_local_target and reused by both. Callers (Run.Worker, Lander.writeback, Lander.Resilience) pass project:. Tests: roadmap/durable_test.exs (interleave, non-ff retry+exhaustion, no-op, local ff-sync, dirty-skip, fallback).

task.title: Per-facet scout-AI competence assessment — replace AND delete the CapabilityScore composite + routing arithmetic
acceptance_criteria: A scout AI reads raw run records grouped by the AI-assigned task facets (from the facet-foundation predecessor) and writes a per-facet competence assessment: for each task-kind, which agent wins on approve-rate / first-try / reviewer-quality / cost, WITH reasoning. Refreshed on a cron or on demand — never a recomputed formula.

dispatch-recommend picks an agent by matching an incoming task's (predicted) facets against that per-facet assessment and returns the choice + the scout's rationale — not by ranking a composite scalar.
AgentKPI is UNCHANGED — it is already pure fact-counting and /harness/kpi depends on it; the deletion is confined to CapabilityScore.

composite_score/4 + every tiebreaker-weight / cost-scale / stale-discount / freshness-window constant removed; freshness / discounted_composite / rebenchmark-candidate / recommend-from-scores reduced to a thin read of the assessment artifact or deleted; corpus_version sha-fingerprinting removed.

No magic weights (0.5/0.3/0.199), no stale_discount, no corpus_version fingerprint, no explore/exploit constants remain in the routing path; mix compile --warnings-as-errors clean; no orphaned ResultStore.save_capability_score callers.
Tests cover: per-facet grouping, the scout assessment read path, dispatch-recommend matching facets, the no-data fallback (unmeasured facet -> explore); CapabilityScore tests updated/removed.
task.body: THE flagship of v0_13, and the actual product: a routing ORACLE answering 'what kind of task goes to which agent?' empirically. A routing oracle is a key->value map: task-kind (the KEY, from the facet-foundation predecessor) -> which agent wins (the VALUE: approve / first-try / reviewer-quality / cost, already captured). Today harness has the value but squashes the per-kind granularity into ONE tunable composite scalar (capability_score.ex:502-533 — ratings+cost+fix-size via hand-tuned weights, freshness decay, corpus fingerprint, explore/exploit branching, 562 LOC) that dispatch-recommend routes on. 'Which agent is best at THIS KIND of work?' is judgment — a scout AI reading the records grouped by facet answers it per-kind and explains itself, where a scalar cannot. Build the per-facet scout assessment + facet-matched routing AND delete the now-orphaned composite in the same change — the build and the deletion are one atomic swap (you cannot satisfy 'no magic weights remain in the routing path' without removing capability_score.ex's arithmetic). Keep ResultStore (raw facts) and AgentKPI (pure counting — the /harness/kpi ledger). The moduledoc itself admits the weights need 'retuning' — that is the tell. (Absorbed former task 217 — the composite deletion was that task's whole deliverable and is already entailed by this task's acceptance criteria.)

task.title: Reviewer rubric foundation — task-kind facets (routing KEY) + two-axis scored skills (routing VALUE) in review.json
acceptance_criteria: review.json gains an optional `facets` block — open-vocabulary AI characterization of what the task ACTUALLY was, read from the task spec + the real diff (e.g. {language, surface, archetype, difficulty, risk}). This is the routing KEY. Reviewer prompt instructs it to emit them.

review.json's flat `ratings` is replaced by a richer two-axis `skills` block — programming domains (otp, ecto, phoenix, liveview, js, rust…) AND cross-cutting qualities (concurrency, error_handling, idiom, test_rigor, security, docs, truthfulness), each {score 0-10, note}, assessed ONLY for skills the diff exercised. This is the richer routing VALUE that replaces the fused 4-key ratings. Legacy flat `ratings` folded in for back-compat.
Both blocks ride the SAME reviewer-prompt change — reviewer_prompt/1 AND reviewer_reprompt/1 in run.ex updated in sync (the prompt is embedded twice).
Harness.Run.Review parses both `facets` and `skills` verbatim (free-form keys/values); a missing block parses to %{} — never a crash, never a closed enum.

Both persist onto Harness.Run.LogRecord + the Postgres run_record schema (open `:map` columns + one additive migration `review_skills`) so they are queryable per-record. Coordinate this migration with the recovery run_record columns (v0_14 AR-seam) to avoid a migration-ordering clash.
facets are GROUND TRUTH from the diff — supersede the sparse, optional, human-assigned `domains` tag as the grouping key (domains may remain a coarse prior).
Tests: facet + skills parse/persist round-trip, missing-block tolerance, legacy-ratings back-compat, and a record carrying both readable back from ResultStore.
task.body: The ROOT of the routing-oracle work — both halves of the key->value map, landed in ONE reviewer-prompt change because they share every file (reviewer_prompt/1 + reviewer_reprompt/1 in run.ex, the review.ex parse, the log_record + run_record persistence). (1) The KEY: today the only task-kind signal is `domains` — optional, human-assigned, sparse (empty for most production tasks). Truthfulness/tokens/quality are OUTCOME axes (value), not task-TYPE axes (key) — you cannot rank 'best at X' without knowing each run WAS an X. 'What kind of task is this?' is judgment, so the reviewer (already reading spec + diff + transcript) writes a `facets` block. (2) The VALUE: today the reviewer emits a flat 4-key `ratings` that CapabilityScore then fuses into one magic-weight number. Replace it with a two-axis `skills` rubric (domains × qualities, each {score, note}, only for skills the diff exercised) — far richer raw facts for an AI to synthesize capability from later, no formula. Both blocks cost near-zero marginal dispatch (the reviewer already runs). Everything downstream — the scout per-facet assessment + composite deletion (216), the KPI pivot (225) — reads these. Open vocabulary, not a maintained enum. (Absorbed the planning-doc's AN-1 'rich agent-skill rubric' — it is the VALUE half of this same change, not a separate task.)

Zero-token mechanical retry on genuinely-transient substrate ops, BEFORE any failure path runs. Retrying a git lock is mechanical counting; it classifies nothing — which keeps it mantra-clean and out of the false-red/false-green class. Independent quick win, parallel to the AI-recovery seam (229).

task.title: Tier-2: the bounded, witnessed AI-recovery seam (.harness/recovery.json) — first call-site checkout pollution
acceptance_criteria: ONE pre-terminal recovery seam: before settling :failed for a NON-rejection reason, spawn a bounded recovery AI with MINIMAL context (error term + git status + transcript tail + failing-check output — never the full transcript) that writes .harness/recovery.json: repaired -> resume the lifecycle / dead -> settle :failed. Harness reads the file mechanically and decides NOTHING about recoverability itself.

First and only initial call-site = checkout pollution (plan gap 5 — the one genuinely interpretive failure; gaps 1/2/3 are Tier-1 retry in 227, gaps 4/6 are mechanical fallbacks in 228). The seam is built generalizable (call-sites can be added later) but ships with exactly one consumer — no generic-for-zero-consumers over-build.
GUARDRAIL: a repaired outcome resumes at a state that RE-RUNS the reviewer gate — never skips to :done. A recovery that commits and resumes past the gate is the false-green class returning.

GUARDRAIL: recovery is bounded PER-RUN (a single run-level recovery budget, not per-failure-type — else N gaps x 1 attempt burns N recovery AIs on one doomed run), and a genuine verdict:reject is NEVER routed through recovery.

WITNESS (folds in the plan's GR-1): persist recovery_attempts, the outcome, what was repaired, AND recovery token spend as raw facts on log_record + the run_record schema (one additive migration). No scoring. The token spend is the metric that proves two-tier is cheaper than hard-fail+manual-redispatch.
Coordinate the run_record migration with task 224's review_skills migration to avoid a migration-ordering clash.
Optionally refactor Task 189's lander resolver and Task 203's re-prompt to be call-sites of this one seam (door left open; not required to land).
No cond/regex error-classifier added to harness (mantra check); the recovery DECISION lives in recovery.json, written by the AI.

Tests: pollute the checkout -> run recovers and re-hits the gate; a genuinely-dead case settles :failed with witnessed recovery_attempts; per-run budget exhaustion fails honestly; verdict:reject bypasses recovery.

Bounded, witnessed, never hides a genuine reject, never resumes past the reviewer gate. The token-spend witness IS the milestone hypothesis test.

task.title: AgentKPI: attribute review_stuck to the reviewer, not the implementer; track per-reviewer verdict-write reliability
acceptance_criteria: AgentKPI exposes a per-reviewer-adapter verdict-write reliability metric: review_stuck count over total reviews that reviewer gated, computed purely from persisted LogRecord fields (reason == {:review_stuck, _} keyed by reviewer_adapter). No new judgment branch/regex/classifier — it only counts a fact already on the record.

A review_stuck run no longer debits the IMPLEMENTER's success_rate: it is excluded from (or counted separately in) the implementer's run_count denominator, because the implementer exited fine and the REVIEWER produced no artifact. Attribution is keyed mechanically on `reason`, not inferred.

The per-reviewer ledger (reviewer_rejection rollup) is extended to surface no-verdict/review_stuck failures alongside rejections — currently it ignores them (only verdict in [:approve,:reject] is counted).

Tests cover: reviewer verdict-write-reliability math; review_stuck excluded from implementer success denominator; review_stuck included in the reviewer reliability rollup. Use NEVER-HIDE-FAILURES assertions (flunk on unexpected), not assert-true-on-any-outcome.

The new reviewer-reliability signal is surfaced wherever AgentKPI is already surfaced (the /harness/kpi dashboard LiveView and the MCP KPI tool), consistent with existing presentation — no net-new design surface.
out_of_scope: Reducing the review_stuck RATE itself (reviewer prompt / timeout / re-prompt-budget tuning) — separate task.
Persisting the reviewer's raw transcript + outcome (kind/exit_status) so killed-vs-clean-exit is distinguishable — separate diagnostic task; this task counts only the already-persisted `reason` fact.
Any capability-routing change that consumes the new reliability signal — file separately once the signal exists.
task.body:
## Observation (the muster, 2026-06-05)
Across 10 persisted review_stuck records (reviewer exited without writing `.harness/review.json`): Cursor 6 / Claude 3 / Pi 1 by reviewer adapter. This is NOT a Cursor bug — Cursor also wrote 38 successful verdicts (it is the most-dispatched reviewer); its 6 are a base-rate-of-use artifact. The failure is cross-family: any reviewer sometimes ends its turn without the mandatory final file write. It correlates with large implementer diffs / long review durations (task 64 = a 21,583-line implementer diff; stuck reviews span 376-1006s).

## The two KPI defects (both confirmed in agent_kpi.ex)
1. IMPLEMENTER penalized for a REVIEWER flake. `agent_kpi.ex:119` sets `passes = verdict == :approve` and `:124` computes `success_rate = passes / run_count`. A review_stuck run has `verdict == nil`, so it sits in the implementer's denominator as a non-pass — e.g. codex (exited 0, real diff) is debited because Cursor wrote no artifact. Since CapabilityScore/routing consume these rates, the distortion mis-routes future dispatch.
2. REVIEWER reliability invisible. The per-reviewer ledger (`agent_kpi.ex:178`) only counts records whose `verdict in [:approve, :reject]`. review_stuck (verdict nil) is excluded entirely, so "did this reviewer write a verdict at all?" is untracked — exactly the signal needed to prefer reliable reviewers.

## Why this belongs in the KPI (mantra check)
review_stuck is a COUNTED FACT — `reason == {:review_stuck, _}`, already persisted on every LogRecord, keyed by `reviewer_adapter`. Rolling it up read-only and fixing attribution (reviewer fact, not implementer fault) is counting + aggregation, NOT judgment. Do not add a classifier, regex, or "is this the reviewer's fault" heuristic — the `reason` field already states the fact; the task only counts and attributes it.

## Approach sketch (non-binding)
- AgentKPI: in the per-agent rollup, partition records so review_stuck is not a non-pass against the implementer (exclude from denominator or report as a separate `reviewer_flaked` count).
- AgentKPI: extend the per-reviewer rollup to count review_stuck (verdict nil + reason review_stuck) as a `no_verdict_rate` alongside `rejection_rate`.
- Surface in /harness/kpi + MCP KPI tool.

Discovered while driving the autocron onchain batch; 6 of the recent failures were review_stuck. Related (separate) follow-ups noted in out_of_scope.

task.title: Persist reviewer raw output + outcome (kind/exit_status) on LogRecord so review_stuck is diagnosable
acceptance_criteria: Harness.Run.Result gains a `reviewer_outcome :: Outcome.t() | nil` field — the reviewer agent's settled %Outcome{} (its raw transcript in .output, plus .kind / .exit_status), or nil when the run never produced a clean reviewer outcome (killed by idle/spawn timeout, crash, or no reviewer available).

run.ex captures the reviewer Outcome that is currently pattern-matched-and-discarded at the `:reviewing` {:ok, %{outcome: %Outcome{}, ...}} clause, stashes it on the gen_statem data, and threads it into build_result. On a Task-203 re-prompt the LAST pass's outcome wins (overwrite, not accumulate).

Harness.Run.LogRecord gains `reviewer_output :: binary()` (default ""), `reviewer_outcome_kind :: Outcome.kind() | nil`, `reviewer_exit_status :: integer() | nil`, populated from result.reviewer_outcome via a put_reviewer_outcome/2 mirroring the existing put_outcome/2. Pure mechanical capture — no interpretation, no classifier.

Tests cover: (a) LogRecord.from_result with a reviewer_outcome populates the three new fields from the Outcome; (b) a nil reviewer_outcome leaves them at defaults; (c) a review_stuck run (clean reviewer exit, no verdict file) persists the reviewer's raw transcript in reviewer_output so the next stuck run is diagnosable. NEVER-HIDE-FAILURES assertions (flunk on unexpected), not assert-true.
out_of_scope: Persisting partial reviewer transcript when the reviewer was KILLED (idle/spawn timeout, crash) — no clean Outcome exists on those paths; reviewer_outcome stays nil and the existing {:review_stuck, report} reason already records which kill path. Capturing the live transcript segment for killed reviewers is a separate, more invasive transcript-segmentation effort.
Any KPI attribution / reviewer-reliability rollup change — that is task 231.
Reducing the review_stuck rate itself (prompt / timeout / re-prompt-budget tuning).
task.body:
## Why (the muster, 2026-06-05)
review_stuck (reviewer exits without writing .harness/review.json) is recurring and cross-family (Claude/Cursor/Pi). Root-causing it is blocked by a diagnostic gap: harness persists the IMPLEMENTER's raw output (agent_output, from the implementer Outcome) but DISCARDS the reviewer's Outcome — it is pattern-matched at run.ex:806 (`{:ok, %{outcome: %Outcome{}, reviewer_diff_size: _, review: _}}`) and never bound. So on a stuck run we have the reason string but not the reviewer's transcript showing WHAT it did before ending its turn without the file write.

## The dominant stuck mode is a CLEAN exit, not a kill
Evidence: stuck runs are SHORTER than successful ones (median ~506s vs ~780s, max 2000s), and stuck median diff (~214) ~= ok (~244). The reviewer is not being timeout-killed mid-review — it reviews, then ends its turn early without the mandatory final write. On that path the reviewer Outcome IS present (Driver.run returned {:ok, %Outcome{}}) with kind=:completed, exit_status, and the full transcript in .output. Capturing it is the highest-value diagnostic and is free — the value is already in hand at run.ex:806, just thrown away.

## Mantra check
Pure mechanics: capture a raw %Outcome{} and copy three fields onto the persisted record, mirroring the implementer side exactly (put_outcome/2). No judgment, no classifier, no regex inferring fault. This persists facts so a future AI (or task 231's rollup) can read them; it does not compute meaning.

## Approach (non-binding)
1. Run.Result: add reviewer_outcome field + typedoc.
2. run.ex: add reviewer_outcome to data struct (type + init nil); bind the outcome in the :reviewing {:ok, ...} clause and stash on data before settle_review; add reviewer_outcome to build_result.
3. LogRecord: add reviewer_output / reviewer_outcome_kind / reviewer_exit_status + put_reviewer_outcome/2; call it in from_result.
4. Tests per acceptance criteria.
task.implemented: Added reviewer_outcome to Run.Result (captured from the previously-discarded reviewer Outcome in the :reviewing settle path) and reviewer_output/reviewer_outcome_kind/reviewer_exit_status to Run.LogRecord (put_reviewer_outcome/2 mirroring put_outcome/2). Postgres schema columns + migration + cast/conflict-merge(COALESCE)/select-strip/row mapping; File backend strips the reviewer_output blob on list scans (point lookup keeps it). Tests: log_record_test (3 cases incl. review_stuck transcript), run_test (approve + review_stuck capture), result_store contract + file/postgres backends. Docs: CHANGELOG + harness-driver SKILL.

task.title: Cron-as-orchestrator-AI — replace roadmap_poller.ex code-driven task selection with a full-context orchestrator AI gated by a mechanical upside-count
acceptance_criteria: A mechanical upside-count gate runs every cron tick (pure counting, no agent): count dispatchable pending tasks (deps done, not handbuild) whose `touches` sets are disjoint enough to batch. Zero/one trivial task -> do NOT wake the orchestrator (fall back to the existing direct dispatch).

When the count shows a batchable cluster, spawn an orchestrator AI WITH FULL CONTEXT (the rmap ready set with bodies/scores/touches/markers/assignee, capability facts) — it is the smart layer, not token-starved. It decides the inline/batch/dispatch grouping and emits the dispatch plan as an artifact harness reads mechanically.

roadmap_poller.ex no longer encodes the next-task / grouping DECISION in code (the @default_agent + assignee cond selection is replaced by reading the orchestrator's plan). Harness still mechanically: counts, fires the timer, reads the plan, enqueues. NOTE: @default_agent = :claude is itself the opus-last-roster violation; the orchestrator must honor each task's stored assignee (cursor/codex/grok preferred, claude reserved) rather than defaulting work to claude.
No cond/regex in harness classifies which tasks to batch — the grouping judgment lives in the orchestrator AI's plan artifact (mantra: count facts in code, write meaning with an AI).
Tests: a tick with no batchable cluster never spawns the orchestrator (zero token cost); a tick with a cluster spawns it once and harness enqueues exactly the plan it wrote.

Stale-base avoidance (the lesson that wide parallel dispatch off one base lacked): the orchestrator's plan must never group tasks whose `touches`/`files_to_modify` overlap EACH OTHER or any IN-FLIGHT run, and must pace dispatch in touch-disjoint waves (a wave lands before the next is planned) so later runs don't rebase across earlier lands. Observed 2026-06-05: a 10-wide batch off one `development` snapshot produced stale-base rebase collisions — 228's reviewer-fn rename silently broke 229's recovery call after both landed (each compiled on its own stale branch; the lander does no re-verify).

The per-project Oban `concurrency_cap` stays the MECHANICAL ceiling beneath the orchestrator: the orchestrator decides which/whether (judgment), the cap enforces how-many and the plan cannot override it. The orchestrator must also account for the SHARED cross-family reviewer pool across cron-enabled projects — concurrent-dispatch sizing considers reviews already in flight on OTHER projects, since the reviewer quota (e.g. Cursor) is global, not per-project.
task.body: Tiny tasks cost a full implement->review->audit ceremony each, so a pile of fragments is token-expensive. roadmap_poller.ex (269 LOC) currently picks the next task and routes it by code (assignee / @default_agent = :claude) — a mechanical selector that cannot judge whether several pending tasks should batch into one dispatch, and whose claude default burns opus tokens against the opus-last roster. Reframe: cron is just a timer (mechanical); what it TRIGGERS should be an orchestrator AI that reads the ready set and decides inline/batch/dispatch grouping with real judgment. CORRECTION (operator, 2026-06-05): the orchestrator is THE SMART LAYER — give it full context, do not token-starve it. The earlier plan-doc instinct to hand it minimal tokens was wrong; constraining the smart guy defeats the point. Token economy comes from the MECHANICAL UPSIDE-COUNT GATE that decides WHETHER to wake it (counting is ~free, mantra-clean), never from crippling its reasoning. The orchestrator never runs for nothing; when it runs, it thinks fully. Sibling to the measure-fragmentation-tax task — that quantifies the tax this saves.
task.implemented: RoadmapPoller gate: pure count classifies the dispatchable ready set (0 nothing / 1 direct-dispatch by assignee / >=2 wake orchestrator). New Harness.Cron.Orchestrator AI (default :codex, configurable) reads ready+in-flight-touches+capability facts, writes .harness/cron-plan.json {dispatch,skip}; harness reads it mechanically (validate in-set, resolve adapter, enqueue), no grouping logic in code. @default_agent=:claude removed (missing/human assignee skipped, not Opus-defaulted). Roadmap.ready/1 gains :fields opt. Empty/malformed plan dispatches nothing (no blind fan-out); wave-pacing via cron cadence + dedup. Hand-built (UI-free, but reshapes the autonomous dispatch runtime). 24 cron tests + dialyzer 0 + credo clean.

task.title: MEASURE the fragmentation / ceremony tax — quantify per-task dispatch overhead from the per-run token facts already captured
acceptance_criteria: A read-only analysis (query or small read fn over the run records / ResultStore) computes the per-task ceremony token cost: implementer + cross-family reviewer + audit token spend per landed task, aggregated across recent runs.
Output is raw facts only (per-task totals, distribution, median/p90) — it ranks nothing and decides nothing (no 'should we batch' verdict in code; that is the orchestrator AI's job).

The result is consumable by an AI (chat/MCP tool or a documented query) so the operator can see whether a real fragmentation tax exists and set the orchestrator's upside-count threshold from data, not a guess.
Tests: the aggregation returns correct per-task totals over a fixture set of run records.
task.body: The cron-orchestrator task is gated on a mechanical upside-count, but we have no measured number for the fragmentation tax it would save. We DO have the data now: every run persists token facts on the run record. This task surfaces the per-task ceremony cost (implementer + reviewer + audit tokens per landed task) as raw aggregated facts — counting only, no verdict. It is the data prerequisite that sets the orchestrator's batch threshold and proves (or disproves) that the tax is real. Cheap, read-only, dispatchable. Sibling to the cron-orchestrator task; NOT a blocker for it (operator: add, don't defer).

task.title: Review-only salvage primitive — re-review a retained branch without re-running the implementer
acceptance_criteria: A dispatch entry (e.g. dispatch-rereview run_id / Dispatch.rereview/1) loads a settled run record, branches a worktree off harness/<run-id>, and starts a Run that enters :reviewing WITHOUT spawning the implementer Port.

The reviewer runs against the existing committed work; approve -> land via the normal lander path; reject/missing -> :failed, task back to queue. Same .harness/review.json verdict contract as a normal run.
A test asserts the implementer phase is genuinely skipped: no implementer invocation, no implementer token spend; only the reviewer runs.
Doc note in dispatch.ex distinguishing rereview (review-stage failure, work is good) from resume_failed (implement-stage failure, continue the work).
out_of_scope: No classifier/heuristic deciding WHICH path to auto-use — the caller picks rereview vs resume_failed explicitly.
No change to the verdict-artifact format or the lander's rebase/ff-push mechanics.
task.body:
When a run fails at the REVIEW stage — `review_stuck` (reviewer died / quota / exited without writing `.harness/review.json`) or a beam-restart cancellation mid-review — but the implementer already committed good work on the retained `harness/<run-id>` branch, the only salvage today is `resume_failed`, which re-runs the IMPLEMENTER off that branch before reviewing again. That pays a full implementer cycle (tokens + wall-clock) to fix a reviewer-side failure where the implementation was never the problem.

Observed repeatedly: this session's 211/221/229 salvage (all review-stage failures with good committed work), plus the earlier 64/76/77/78/79/219 `review_stuck` batch. Every one re-spent an implementer cycle it did not need.

Add a review-only path: take a settled run (or a retained `harness/<run-id>` branch) + its task, seed a worktree from the branch, and enter the `Harness.Run` gen_statem directly in `:reviewing` — skipping the `:running`/implementer phase entirely — producing a verdict and landing on approve via the normal lander path.

Mechanical only (THE MANTRA): no judgment is added. The caller decides rereview-vs-resume_failed; harness just offers a lifecycle entry that starts at the gate instead of at the implementer. resume_failed stays for the implement-failed case; this is the review-failed case.

acceptance_criteria: Harness.Cron.Settings: per-project dispatch mode (:auto|:manual), absence => :auto (existing autonomous projects keep auto-dispatching, zero behavior change); persisted via SettingsStore write-through + seeded by load_into_env/0; runtime setter with actor audit log, mirroring set_project/3.
Poller: under :manual, BOTH direct_dispatch and the orchestrator-plan enqueue park instead of enqueueing; under :auto, behavior is byte-identical to today.
Pending-approval store + dispatch-approve MCP tool (and a dispatch-pending listing tool) that enqueues a parked record; approval is idempotent.
Harness.Notification witness event on park (read-only sink, never a gate).
Tests cover both modes on both the 1-task and >=2-task paths, the park->approve->enqueue round-trip, and that interactive dispatch is ungated.

Auto-approving any run by heuristic (judgment -> not harness code).

task.body:
Add a per-project cron DISPATCH MODE — `:auto` (default, today's behavior) | `:manual`
— as a third dimension in `Harness.Cron.Settings`, parallel to the existing on/off
`:cron_project_autonomy` boolean. Mode only matters when a project is `effective?/1`
(master AND project enabled).

Under `:manual`, the poller's autonomous dispatch does NOT call `Worker.enqueue`. Both
autonomous paths are gated at the SAME enqueue boundary: 1 dispatchable task
(`direct_dispatch`) and >=2 tasks (the orchestrator AI's `.harness/cron-plan.json`
plan). Instead of enqueuing, harness PARKS the decision (task ids + resolved adapters)
as a pending-approval record and fires a `Harness.Notification` witness event. An
operator `dispatch-approve` action drains the parked record into `Worker.enqueue`,
after which the normal implement->review->land loop runs unchanged.

MANTRA-clean: purely MECHANICAL. The orchestrator AI still makes ALL the judgment
(which tasks, which adapter, touch-disjoint, opus-last); the manual gate only HOLDS the
mechanical enqueue until an operator approves. No "is this run high-stakes" classifier
— the gate keys solely off the per-project mode flag.

Interactive `dispatch-task` / `dispatch-await` are NOT gated — the operator already
chose to issue those; only the autonomous (cron) path is parked.

Motivation: cron dispatch runs inside the OTP node, so a Claude Code hook cannot gate
it. The existing master/per-project toggles are coarse on/off; this is the middle
ground — let the orchestrator plan the wave, but approve before anything spawns (useful
when claude/opus is in the planned adapter set under autonomy). Deferred / low priority
(eff 0.83): the coarse kill-switch already covers the safety case; this only buys the
plan-but-approve middle ground. Sibling to Task 233 (the orchestrator) — same cron
dispatch path.

task.title: Fix MCP dispatch-hold boolean-arg coercion + document hold→steer→resume recovery in harness-driver SKILL
acceptance_criteria: mcp__harness__dispatch-hold with interrupt:true (and interrupt:false) reaches Harness.Dispatch.hold/2 successfully — no is_boolean guard failure; covered by a test that exercises the MCP/tools arg path, not just the runtime function.
The arg coercion is at the MCP/tools binding boundary (or via a typed param declaration), not by loosening the is_boolean guard on Harness.Dispatch.hold/2.

skills/harness-driver/SKILL.md documents the hold→steer→resume recovery pattern: steer is async (next-boundary only); to redirect a live turn pair it with hold(interrupt)→resume; the over-grinding-implementer force-handoff reframe (reviewer runs/fixes the gate, implementer needn't green it).
No new mechanical judgment in harness code — the doc describes operator use of existing mechanical primitives.
out_of_scope: Changing hold/resume/steer semantics
Adding the implementer idle watchdog (separate task)
task.body:
Two coupled deliverables on the operator-recovery driver surface.

BUG (hit live 2026-06-06, run-1780714000066-f7d737a3): calling the MCP tool `mcp__harness__dispatch-hold` with `interrupt: true` throws `no function clause matching in Harness.Dispatch.hold/2` — the `def hold(run_id, interrupt \\ false) when is_binary(run_id) and is_boolean(interrupt)` guard rejects the value the MCP/descripex arg-binding passes (a non-boolean — string "true" or wrapped map). Direct runtime call `Harness.Dispatch.hold(run_id, true)` works, which is the workaround used mid-incident. So an orchestrator driving harness over MCP cannot interrupt a wedged/over-grinding run — the recovery primitive is broken on the public surface. Trace where the MCP layer binds the `interrupt` JSON arg and coerce it to a boolean (or declare the param type so descripex coerces), so the MCP path reaches the same guarded function the runtime call does.

DOC (coupled — same recovery surface; CLAUDE.md mandates SKILL updates on driver-surface changes): document the hold→steer→resume operator-recovery pattern in skills/harness-driver/SKILL.md. Two non-obvious facts proven this session: (1) `dispatch-steer` is ASYNC — it stashes a note that only threads in at the next agent boundary, so to redirect a LIVE agent turn you must pair it with `hold(interrupt) → resume`; steer alone never reaches a continuous grind. (2) The reframe that made it work: an implementer that over-grinds the gate (loops re-running `mix precommit` trying to green it before committing) does NOT need to pass the gate — the cross-family reviewer runs and fixes the checks inline. So the operator move for an over-grinding implementer is force-handoff: hold(interrupt) → steer("commit your work and hand off; you don't need to green precommit") → resume. Worked example: task 216 cursor looped precommit ~7x (3 FAILED) on ~15 lines of polish; hold→steer→resume flipped it to :reviewing in <1 min, codex reviewer hardened + approved → landed.

task.title: Implementer-phase idle watchdog — a wedged :running agent holds a queue slot up to the 90-min lifetime cap
acceptance_criteria: The implementer :running phase enforces an idle watchdog: a run whose agent emits no port output for the idle window settles (fail/rotate) instead of waiting for the 90-min lifetime cap.

The idle floor is high enough that a single silent check_command run (compile + full test + dialyzer) does not trip it — mirror the reviewer floor's rationale; an explicit higher idle_timeout opt still wins.
Watchdog resets on each transcript chunk (last-activity timer), purely mechanical — no classifier deciding whether the agent is stuck.
Test: a run with a stubbed agent that goes silent past the floor settles via the watchdog; a run emitting periodic output past the floor does not.
out_of_scope: The MCP dispatch-hold bug + recovery doc (separate task)
Changing the 90-min lifetime cap or the reviewer idle floor
task.body:
Confirmed empirically 2026-06-06 (task 216, run-1780712414298-… and run-1780714000066-…): the implementer `:running` phase has NO idle watchdog. `idle_timeout` resolves to `nil` by default (config.ex {:run, :idle_timeout} default is nil), and the driver treats nil as "no idle limit", so a wedged implementer (cursor-agent sitting at 0% CPU, transcript flat) is only caught by the 90-min `lifetime_timeout` backstop. Twice this session a cursor implementer wedged and sat until manual `hold`/cancel intervention — nothing auto-reaped it, and it held the project queue slot the whole time.

Asymmetry to fix: the REVIEWING phase already has a deliberate 10-min idle floor (`@reviewer_idle_floor`, Task 181) precisely because the reviewer streams nothing for minutes while running the project checks. The IMPLEMENTER has the identical property (it runs `mix`/`cargo` silently for minutes) but no equivalent floor. Add a mechanical idle watchdog to the implementer phase mirroring the reviewer floor: reset on each port chunk, settle/rotate the run when no output for the idle window, with a floor high enough that a single silent check (compile+test+dialyzer) can't trip it. This is pure mechanics — count ms since last chunk, compare to a threshold; no judgment about whether the agent is "really" stuck. The threshold catches a genuinely-wedged agent in minutes instead of holding a slot for up to 90.
